title: Digestive system
summary: How is food broken down, where is it digested, and how does it reach the blood?
cards.0.p: Digestion is the breaking of large food molecules into small units that can cross membranes. Mechanical digestion makes food physically smaller. In chemical digestion, enzymes break bonds by hydrolysis.
cards.0.svg#4: pieces get smaller, structure stays the same
cards.0.svg#6: the enzyme breaks a bond: hydrolysis
cards.0.key: Mechanical digestion increases the surface area, but only chemical digestion changes the molecule. In an amoeba digestion happens inside the cell, and in humans it happens outside the cells.
cards.0.once.soru: Why can't the starch we eat go straight into the blood?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Starch is made of thousands of glucose units. It must first be split into glucose to cross a membrane.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Starch does not disappear in the stomach. Its digestion is completed in the small intestine.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Starch is an important source of energy.
cards.1.h: The digestive tract and accessory organs
cards.1.p: Food moves through a one-way tube. This tube is made of the mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and anus, in that order. Accessory organs release their secretions into this tube.
cards.1.svg#13: food does not pass through these,
cards.1.key: The salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas are not part of the tube. Food does not pass through them.
cards.1.etk.soru: Put in order the path food takes through the digestive tract.
cards.2.p: Teeth grind food, and this mechanical digestion increases the surface area. Saliva makes the bite slippery and contains salivary amylase. That is why the chemical digestion of starch starts in the mouth.
cards.2.svg#11: short time in the mouth: digestion stays partial
cards.2.key: Amylase breaks starch down into maltose. That is why bread starts to taste sweet if you chew it for a long time.
cards.3.p: When you swallow, the epiglottis closes the windpipe. The esophagus does not release enzymes. The bite is pushed to the stomach by wave-like contractions of ring-shaped muscles. This movement is called peristalsis.
cards.3.svg#0: Peristalsis: a wave of ring muscles
cards.3.svg#7: No gravity needed: you can swallow upside down too.
cards.3.key: If food goes down the windpipe, you cough. Peristalsis happens all the way from the esophagus to the anus.
cards.3.once.soru: Can you drink water while upside down?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: The bite is moved by the muscles of the esophagus, not by gravity.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: The esophagus can push liquid upward too, with waves of muscle.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: What matters here is muscle movement, not speed.
cards.4.p: The stomach releases HCl, and the pH inside drops to about 2. HCl turns pepsinogen into pepsin, so protein digestion starts in the stomach. Mucus protects the stomach wall from the acid.
cards.4.key: Stomach acid kills most microbes. Chyme passes little by little through the pylorus into the small intestine. No nutrients are absorbed in the stomach.
cards.4.once.soru: The stomach releases such strong acid. Why doesn't it digest itself?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: The mucus lining the stomach wall keeps acid and pepsin away from it.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: The acid is in the stomach cavity. Without protection it would damage the wall.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: If the mucus breaks down, the stomach wall is digested and an ulcer forms.
cards.5.p: The first part of the small intestine is called the duodenum. The bicarbonate in pancreatic juice neutralizes the acid coming from the stomach. Of the pancreatic enzymes, amylase digests starch, trypsin digests protein and lipase digests fat.
cards.5.key: Bile also flows into the duodenum. The pancreas is a mixed gland, because it also releases insulin and glucagon into the blood.
cards.6.p: Protein-digesting enzymes are released as inactive precursors so they do not digest the cells that make them. In the stomach, HCl activates pepsinogen. In the duodenum, enterokinase activates trypsinogen, and trypsin then activates the other enzymes.
cards.6.svg#14: pepsin is activated in the stomach, the rest in the duodenum
cards.6.key: Trypsin activates chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase. Without enterokinase, this chain never starts.
cards.6.once.soru: Why does the pancreas release trypsin in an inactive form (trypsinogen)?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Active trypsin would also break down the proteins of the pancreatic cells that make it.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: An inactive enzyme does not work. It has to be activated first.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.yazi: So it travels in the blood
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: Trypsinogen is sent to the intestine through a duct, not into the blood.
cards.7.h: The liver, bile and the gallbladder
cards.7.p: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gallbladder. Bile is not an enzyme. It breaks fat into tiny droplets, which is called emulsification. This increases the surface where lipase can work.
cards.7.key: The liver stores extra glucose as glycogen and also neutralizes alcohol and drugs. If the bile duct is blocked, fat digestion fails.
cards.8.p: Maltase, sucrase and lactase in the lining of the small intestine split disaccharides. Peptidases split short peptides into amino acids. The chemical digestion of all foods is completed in the small intestine.
cards.8.key: Each disaccharide is split into two monosaccharides using one molecule of water. Nucleic acids are split by nuclease released from the pancreas.
cards.8.once.soru: Which enzyme breaks down lactose, the sugar in milk?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: Lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose.
cards.9.p: Chemical digestion starts in the mouth for carbohydrates, in the stomach for proteins and in the small intestine for fats. All of them finish in the small intestine. Vitamins, minerals and water are absorbed without being digested.
cards.9.svg#22: Vitamins, minerals and water are absorbed undigested.
cards.9.key: The end products of digestion are monosaccharides, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol. After a fatty meal, the stomach empties more slowly.
cards.9.etk.soru: Match each enzyme or secretion with what it acts on.
cards.10.p: Villi and microvilli greatly increase the absorbing surface. Glucose and amino acids pass into the capillary blood and travel to the liver through the hepatic portal vein. Most fatty acids and glycerol pass into the lymph.
cards.10.key: Glucose and amino acids are absorbed by active transport, and water by osmosis. Thanks to the hepatic portal vein, toxic substances are neutralized in the liver first.
cards.11.p: The large intestine does not release enzymes. It absorbs the remaining water and minerals and turns the leftovers into feces. The helpful bacteria living there make vitamin K and some B vitamins.
cards.11.key: Long-term antibiotic use can also reduce the helpful bacteria.
cards.11.once.soru: Why does the body lose water quickly with diarrhea?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.yazi: The large intestine can't absorb water
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: The leftovers pass through the large intestine too quickly. So the water is expelled before it can be absorbed.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: The stomach releases acid and enzymes. The main place of water loss is the large intestine.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: With diarrhea, gut movement does not stop. It speeds up.
cards.12.p: Seeing or smelling food starts secretion through nerves. Gastrin increases gastric juice. Secretin makes the pancreas release bicarbonate. Cholecystokinin contracts the gallbladder and empties the bile.
cards.12.key: Gastrin is released by the stomach. Secretin is released by the duodenum when acidic chyme arrives.
cards.12.once.soru: What makes your mouth water when you smell food?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: The smell reaches the brain, and the brain stimulates the salivary glands through nerves.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: There is no food in the stomach yet, so hormones have not stepped in.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: The pancreas does not control saliva.
cards.13.p: A sore that opens in the stomach when the mucus breaks down is called an ulcer. When stomach contents flow back into the esophagus, it is called reflux. People with lactose intolerance have little lactase. High-fiber foods prevent constipation.
cards.13.svg#1: a sore in the stomach or
cards.13.svg#14: but it keeps the gut moving,
cards.13.key: Ulcers are mostly caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori or by frequent use of painkillers. In someone with lactose intolerance, milk causes gas and diarrhea.
cards.13.once.soru: Is the cellulose (fiber) we can't digest wasted?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.yazi: No, it keeps the gut moving
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: Fiber increases gut movement and prevents constipation.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: Even though cellulose is not digested, it helps gut movement.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: Cellulose is not digested, so it is not absorbed.
cards.14.p:
• Mechanical digestion breaks food apart, and in chemical digestion enzymes carry out hydrolysis.
• Carbohydrate digestion starts in the mouth, protein in the stomach and fat in the small intestine. All of them finish in the small intestine.
• Bile is not an enzyme. It emulsifies fat.
• Glucose and amino acids pass from the villi into the blood, and fats into the lymph. The large intestine absorbs water.
quiz.0.q: Put each enzyme under the food group it digests.
quiz.0.e: Amylase breaks down starch, and maltase and lactase break down disaccharides. Pepsin, trypsin and peptidases digest proteins, and lipase digests fats.
quiz.1.q: Put in order what happens to a protein until it is digested and absorbed.
quiz.1.ogeler.0: In the stomach, HCl turns pepsinogen into pepsin
quiz.1.ogeler.1: Pepsin splits the protein into short polypeptides
quiz.1.ogeler.4: Peptidases split short peptides into amino acids
quiz.1.ogeler.5: Amino acids pass into the capillary blood of the villus
quiz.1.e: Protein digestion starts in the stomach with pepsin. In the duodenum, enterokinase activates trypsin, and trypsin activates chymotrypsin. Peptidases on the microvillus membrane take the last step, and the amino acids are absorbed into the blood.
quiz.2.q: Match each secretion with its job.
quiz.2.e: Gastrin increases gastric juice, and secretin increases the pancreas's bicarbonate release. Cholecystokinin contracts the gallbladder. Bile emulsifies fat, and bicarbonate neutralizes the acid of the chyme.
quiz.3.q: Someone has had their gallbladder removed by surgery. What becomes hardest for them?
quiz.3.o.0: Digesting fats after a fatty meal
quiz.3.o.3: Absorbing water in the large intestine
quiz.3.e: The liver keeps making bile, but it cannot be stored. So after a fatty meal, not enough bile arrives at once and fat digestion becomes harder.
quiz.3.y.1: Starch digestion in the mouth is done by salivary amylase. Bile only plays a role in emulsifying fats.
quiz.3.y.2: Protein digestion in the stomach is done by pepsin and HCl. Bile emulsifies fats.
quiz.3.y.3: Water absorption in the large intestine does not depend on bile. Bile helps digest fats.
A:ozet: Follow a bite from the mouth to the anus, break down food, run enzymes at the right pH and open up the surface of the villi.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Food travels through a one-way tube that runs from the mouth to the anus. Next to this tube are the accessory organs. Make a guess first, then follow the bite.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which one does the bite not pass through?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The stomach is part of the digestive tract. Here the bite is churned with acid and turns into a soupy mix called chyme.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The esophagus pushes the bite to the stomach by peristalsis. So the bite does pass through it.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The pancreas is an accessory organ, and food does not pass through it. The pancreas releases its juice into the duodenum. The liver works the same way.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Break the bite into pieces and make its surface 4 times larger.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: The more pieces you cut each edge into, the larger the total surface.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: You cut the bite into 64 pieces and made its surface 4 times larger. The surface amylase can touch grew, but the substance is still starch.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Change the food and play all three. Then think about the case below.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: In someone whose salivary glands do not work, what happens to the chemical digestion of starch?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Pancreatic juice also contains amylase. So starch is still digested in the small intestine.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: It starts in the small intestine
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The early digestion in the mouth does not happen. But pancreatic amylase and maltase still break starch down to glucose in the small intestine.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: It starts in the stomach with pepsin
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Pepsin acts only on proteins. The enzyme that breaks down starch is amylase.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Pepsin and trypsin work at different pH values. Change the pH and find where pepsin works fastest.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.ipucu: Pepsin works in the stomach. Stomach acid makes the pH very low.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: At pH 2, pepsin works fastest, while trypsin has almost stopped. Every enzyme has its own optimum pH. When the conditions change, one stops and the other starts working.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Fat forms big drops in water. Lipase can only work on the surface of a drop. Bile, made by the liver, flows into the duodenum. Turn bile on and press play.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.ipucu: Bile breaks fat into tiny droplets. With more surface, lipase works faster.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: Bile broke the fat into tiny droplets. As the surface grew, lipase sped up and broke down all of the fat in the same time.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Most absorption happens in the small intestine. If the small intestine were a smooth tube, its surface would be very small. Fold the wall, then add the villi and microvilli.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.ipucu: At the last level, the membrane of each lining cell forms brush-like projections.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: Folds, villi and microvilli together increase the surface hundreds of times. The maltase, lactase and peptidases on the microvillus membrane also carry out the last step of digestion here.
A:adimlar.6.metin: Inside each villus there is a network of blood capillaries and, in the middle, a lymph capillary with a closed end. Make a guess first, then press play.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: In the villus, where do most fatty acids and glycerol go?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Fatty acids and glycerol are rebuilt into fat in the lining cell, and most of it passes into the lymph. Vitamins A, D, E and K follow this route too. The lymph later joins the blood.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Glucose, amino acids, water and water-soluble vitamins pass into the blood capillary. This blood goes to the liver first. Most fats do not take this route.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The large intestine releases no digestive enzymes and only absorbs water and minerals. Fat is fully digested and absorbed in the small intestine.
A:kapanis.0: Food moves through a one-way tube. The liver and pancreas are not part of the tube, they only release their secretions into it.
A:kapanis.1: Mechanical digestion increases the surface. Only enzymes change the molecule, by hydrolysis.
A:kapanis.2: Chemical digestion starts in the mouth for carbohydrates, in the stomach for proteins and in the small intestine for fats. All of them finish in the small intestine.
A:kapanis.3: Pepsin works in an acidic environment, and pancreatic enzymes work where bicarbonate has neutralized the acid. Bile is not an enzyme, it emulsifies fat.
A:kapanis.4: Villi and microvilli greatly increase the surface. Glucose and amino acids pass into the blood, and most fats into the lymph.
